class_id: Organizational Subject Identity and Registry Anchors
claim_summary: Defines the wallet, owner identification data, and owner as the identity-bearing organisational subject layer for economic operators and public sector bodies.

class_id: Organizational Subject Identity and Registry Anchors
claim_summary: Requires owner identification data to be issued to wallet owners, tied to authentic sources, formatted as EAA/QEAA-type objects, and to contain at least official name plus relevant unique identifier.

class_id: Organizational Subject Identity and Registry Anchors
claim_summary: Makes EUID the default identifier where available and requires a unique identifier scheme, including anti-duplication measures, for owners without EUIDs.

class_id: Organizational Subject Identity and Registry Anchors
claim_summary: Establishes the European Digital Directory as trusted information source for wallet owners, with API and authenticated user interfaces, restricted access, and one-working-day update duties.

class_id: Organizational Subject Identity and Registry Anchors
claim_summary: Explains why BRIS/BORIS and EUID anchors are not sufficient for the whole target population, especially public bodies, sole traders, self-employed persons, and other entities not covered by existing registers.

class_id: Organizational Subject Identity and Registry Anchors
claim_summary: Frames owner identity as a trust-and-register problem built on authentic sources, BRIS/BORIS where useful, and a Digital Directory that should not duplicate business-register information.

class_id: Organizational Subject Identity and Registry Anchors
locator: Article 8(7), Article 9(4), Article 10(6), PDF pp. 38-40 / EN 37-39
claim_summary: Delegates detailed requirements for owner identification data, unique identifiers, unique digital addresses, and Digital Directory information categories to implementing acts.

class_id: Organizational Subject Identity and Registry Anchors
claim_summary: Leaves the legal basis and practical verification mechanism for newly registered or broader non-company entity populations as a remaining issue, including possible phased approaches for public administrations and other groups.
Defines authorised representative and mandate as authority objects separate from owner identity.
Makes multi-user access, operation, relying-party request authorisation, and owner revocation of such authorisations core wallet functions.
Requires access-control decisions to use acting-subject attestations, formal role, mandate scope/validity/constraints, and policy context, with auditable and real-time enforcement.
Delegates role/attribute formats, mandate/delegation interoperability, policy language, constraint enforcement, secure logging, timestamping, and auditability standards to implementing acts.
Identifies the lack of a standardised EU-wide digital mechanism for storing, exchanging, and verifying mandates and powers of attorney as a central burden and risk.
Interprets the EUBW as a digital PoA and mandate-management layer that should issue, revoke, track, and audit representation rights while reducing manual verification.

States that delegation and representation also depend on statutory and legal requirements that the SWD and proposal do not address, leaving legal-authority substance outside the wallet requirement layer.
Defines EAA/QEAA objects, wallet unit attestations, attestations from authentic sources, authentic sources, and attestation schemes.
Makes issuance, request, storage, selective disclosure, presentation, cross-wallet sharing, and linked chains of attestations part of the core functional semantics.
Treats owner identification data itself as an attestation-format object with minimum attributes and an attestation scheme.
Requires EAAs issued to wallet units to comply with listed standards, issuer self-identification by access certificate, and inclusion of information needed for authentication and validation.

Shows the attestation space as broader than identity: licences, certificates, compliance data, VAT, beneficial ownership, procurement, CE conformity, and other business credentials need exchangeable semantics.
Explains linked attestations as reusable documentation, allowing information to remain reliable and trusted across procedures without resubmission.
Delegates the reference standards, specifications, and procedures for core attestation functions to implementing acts.

locator: Annex point 12(4)(a) and point 17(1), PDF pp. 7-8 / EN 6-7
claim_summary: Leaves concrete role/attribute representation formats and EAA technical standards to implementing-act standard lists rather than fixing them in the proposal or annex.

class_id: Credential Lifecycle, Exchange, and Event State
claim_summary: Frames lifecycle and exchange through storing, deleting, sharing, QERDS transmission, data export, transaction logs, and a communication dashboard.

class_id: Credential Lifecycle, Exchange, and Event State
claim_summary: Requires wallet validity revocation in specified circumstances and public notification of validation mechanisms.

class_id: Credential Lifecycle, Exchange, and Event State
claim_summary: Requires a public revocation policy for wallet unit attestations, user notice within 24 hours, and public validity-status information.

class_id: Credential Lifecycle, Exchange, and Event State
claim_summary: Specifies transaction logs covering signatures, seals, notifications, counterparties, requested/presented data, failed transactions, integrity/confidentiality, provider access, and legally required retention.

class_id: Credential Lifecycle, Exchange, and Event State
claim_summary: Requires secure export and portability of owner wallet data in at least an open format with assurance at least substantial.

class_id: Credential Lifecycle, Exchange, and Event State
claim_summary: Specifies issuance, delivery, activation, authenticity/validity verification, and cryptographic binding of owner identification data and attestations to wallet units.

class_id: Credential Lifecycle, Exchange, and Event State
claim_summary: Stakeholders read lifecycle control as requiring register updates, real-time validation, validity-period handling, and revocation mechanisms for credentials and powers of attorney.

class_id: Credential Lifecycle, Exchange, and Event State
claim_summary: Connects lifecycle/event state to business traceability, ERP/KYC integration, audit gaps, and tracking of shared attributes in professional contexts.

class_id: Credential Lifecycle, Exchange, and Event State
claim_summary: Leaves concrete log retention duration to Union or national law rather than fixing an EUBW-specific retention period.
Requires providers to be listed, Union-established, not controlled by high-risk third-country actors, and compliant with eIDAS, NIS2, cybersecurity, and supplier-security requirements.
Creates a notification mechanism for wallet providers, including required provider information, functionality descriptions, conformity declarations, review timelines, and judicial remedy.
Requires Commission-maintained machine-readable listing of notified providers based on supervisory-body information.

Allocates supervision to eIDAS supervisory bodies, including notification review, investigations, remedy duties, breach cooperation, penalties, provider removal, and Commission emergency intervention.
Extends the European Digital Identity Cooperation Group and sets Commission supervision for Union-entity wallet providers.
Provides a third-country equivalence mechanism for similar business wallets or frameworks based on interoperability and functional assurance.

locator: Sections 5 and 5.1, PDF pp. 29-30 / internal pp. 28-29
claim_summary: Interprets EUBW as a coherent extension of the EUDI framework, not a separate framework, with interoperability between EUDI Wallets and EUBWs as a defining principle.
Reports stakeholder pressure for regulation to focus on trustworthy verifiable credentials, legal effect, interoperability, open standards, and provider competition rather than rigid wallet design.

locator: Recital 40 and Article 11(4)-(6), PDF pp. 23-24 and 40-41 / EN 22-23 and 39-40
claim_summary: The assurance model is mainly streamlined notification and ex post supervision; the proposal does not create full prior compliance verification for every provider operation.

Requires common protocols and interfaces for issuance, relying-party requests, sharing, automated interaction, remote onboarding, EUDI/EUBW interaction, relying-party authentication, QERDS, digital addresses, unit attestations, and critical assets.

Requires owner ID association, interoperable and auditable role mappings, real-time prevention of conflicts/over-delegation/expired authorisations, security by design, validation mechanisms, and support/reporting channels.

Specifies user authentication, wallet-unit integrity, secure back-end/front-end/cryptographic-device communication, critical-asset management, and secure cryptographic application/device capabilities.

Requires mandatory integration with a specific QERDS as secure legal communication channel, with open standards, end-to-end encryption, availability, redundancy, fallback, and provider technical integration.

Requires protocol/interface support for request authorisation, relying-party or unit authentication, user display of certificate/attestation information, requested attributes, and presentation of wallet unit attestations.
Requires presentation protocols and interfaces to relying parties and proof of possession of private keys corresponding to cryptographic bindings.
Makes machine-readable export, transaction-log access, and common dashboard access core operational controls for enterprise use.
Interprets EUBW operational value through ERP/CRM and core business application integration, secure APIs, portability, no vendor lock-in, and future readiness for AI or asset identity.
Stakeholders expect multiple implementation models, including mobile, enterprise-integrated, and cloud solutions, based on open interoperable standards and integration with existing business systems.
Delegates detailed standards, specifications, and procedures for technical features to implementing acts.
Leaves operational viability dependent on integration quality, usability, minimal user interaction, training, and adoption readiness, especially for SMEs and larger enterprises with existing systems.
The 1/2 boundary holds because owner identification data and mandates are separately defined as identity versus authority concepts.
The 1/2 boundary strains because a single access-control decision combines acting-subject attestations, formal role, mandate scope/validity/constraints, and policy context.
The 1/2 boundary strains in practice because multi-layered representation and internal mandates can make identity and authority verification inseparable in cross-border operations.
The 3/4 boundary holds because the proposal separately defines credential and attestation object types before lifecycle handling.
The 3/4 boundary holds because the annex separately specifies revocation policy, validity status, transaction logging, and retention as lifecycle/event-state requirements.

locator: Recital 27 and Article 5(1)(g), PDF pp. 20-21 and 33 / EN 19-20 and 32
claim_summary: The 3/4 boundary strains because linked attestations are both an object-semantic structure and a reuse/exchange lifecycle mechanism.
The 3/4 boundary strains because issuance provisions combine format support, delivery, activation, authenticity, and validity checks in one operational cluster.
The 5/6 boundary holds because notification, provider listing, supervisory tasks, penalties, and Commission intervention are institutional-governance mechanisms.

locator: Annex points 1-4 and 11, PDF pp. 2-6 / EN 1-5
claim_summary: The 5/6 boundary holds because authentication, cryptographic devices, secure communication, QERDS integration, redundancy, and fallback are operational-control requirements.

locator: Article 7(4)-(5) and Article 6(2)(c), PDF pp. 35-37 / EN 34-36
claim_summary: The 5/6 boundary strains because provider governance imports cybersecurity, high-risk-supplier, and security-by-design obligations that directly shape operational architecture and supply-chain control.

The 5/6 boundary strains because stakeholders want legal-effect/interoperability governance without rigid architecture, while also expecting access controls, audit logs, traceability, and fraud safeguards as standard features.
Market-driven deployment, paid service models, fair competition, and provider ecosystem design are important to uptake but are not cleanly wallet requirement classes.
SME price sensitivity, free implementation demands, provider pricing models, training, and adoption readiness belong mainly to rollout economics rather than the six wallet requirement classes.

locator: Annex 3 section 1, PDF pp. 78-80 / internal pp. 77-79
claim_summary: Cost and benefit estimates for microenterprises, SMEs, corporates, PSBs, and providers support business-case framing but do not alter the core class model.
Regulatory evaluation and review duties are relevant to monitoring the initiative but sit outside the core wallet-requirement classes unless used narrowly for governance context.

Monitoring indicators for administrative burden, public service delivery, competitiveness, provider counts, penalties, and wallets issued are meta-evaluation material rather than wallet class substance.

Penalty scales and exceptional Commission corrective/restrictive measures are enforcement mechanics; they support trust governance but are residual if the paper is deriving wallet requirement classes.
